column4: Tap the steady beat, then hear which instrument moves freely across it.
Listen for overlapping trumpet and clarinet melodies instead of a single lead.
Find an answer from another instrument after a short phrase.
Follow the bass line as it moves one step per beat through changing chords.
Notice a soloist sounding slightly late without losing the underlying pulse.
Ignore the solo for ten seconds; focus on bass, drums and chordal support.
Listen for bent notes and phrases that feel closer to a sung voice.
Find a phrase repeated with one small rhythmic or melodic change.
Listen for the underlying song form when a new solo begins.
Notice a trumpet or trombone line answered by the saxophones.
Hear a band accenting a phrase together before another solo.
Find a few piano notes that leave room for the other musicians.
Listen for syllables that float across the beat.
Notice a vocal phrase imitating a horn or a drum figure.
Follow a bebop run, then notice its punctuation and breath.
Hear a short drum accent responding to a soloist.
Listen for a pause that changes the meaning of the next note.
Find a passage where several instruments blend without dominating.
Hear how gospel-like accents or blues phrases ground complex harmony.
Listen for a solo exploring one tonal color for several measures.
Hear how a saxophonist builds intensity through repeated ideas.
Try to hear which player proposes an idea and who replies.
Count carefully; do the accents line up with the dance pulse?
Focus on the relationship of congas to drum kit and bass.
Hear the understated syncopation without assuming the tune is swing.
Compare a Latin rhythmic pattern with a walking jazz bass.
Listen for keyboards or electric guitar changing the band's texture.
Keep one groove in mind while a soloist moves around it.
Write down one unexpected instrument or phrase you heard today.
Notice one difference in the rhythm or ensemble of two jazz broadcasts.
